## A memory is a few thousand hard locations that vote (HOW AN SDM WORKS)

The simplest version, five steps in Kanerva’s own words with pictures, is at the top of SDM EXPLORE. This section is the same memory in more detail.

A sparse distributed memory stores long words of bits. It owns a few thousand **hard locations**. Each hard location has a fixed random address, as long as a word, and a row of bit-counters, one per bit. To write a word, the memory wakes every hard location whose address is close to the word and adds the word to their bit-counters. To read, you give the memory a **read-address**: a word, or a noisy copy of one, which is then a read-address with **address-noise**. The hard locations close to the read-address are activated, their bit-counters are added up bit by bit, and each bit of the answer is the sign of its sum. Kanerva calls the read-address the *retrieval address*, and also the *retrieval cue*; the older lane reports say cue.

Why it works: a noisy address near a stored word wakes most of the hard locations that word was written to. Their bit-counters agree with each other and outvote the other words, which were written to other hard locations. Reading the answer again moves it closer still. Below, the whole thing on a memory of 1,200 hard locations: write a word, make a noisy copy of it, read from that.

The memory is called **sparse** because its locations are a tiny sample of all possible addresses, and **distributed** because every word is spread over many hard locations and every hard location holds a blend of many words.

Sources: P. Kanerva, *Sparse Distributed Memory*, MIT Press, 1988. The equations are the ones the SDMSCALE lane states in its report (section 2). The same memory, drawn as a machine you can run, is on the SDM explore page; the three memories side by side are on the memory page.
